newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO, Serb generals meet amid tensions over raid.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Serb generals meet amid tensions over raid.

text.p: A senior officer in the NATO-led peace force held talks with the commander of the Bosnian Serb army on Monday to try to defuse tensions following a NATO raid on indicted war criminals last week.
Bosnian Serb leaders have condemned the swoop carried out by British special forces against two Serbs wanted by the United Nations war crimes tribunal.
One suspect was arrested and another suspect was shot dead after he opened fire on British soldiers as he tried to escape.

British Lieutenant-General Roddy Cordy-Simpson met General Pero Colic in Bijeljina for 90 minutes and received assurances that the army would seek to keep the situation calm, NATO spokesman Colonel Steven Rausch told Reuters.
Cordy-Simpson described the meeting as "honest and practical", Rausch said.
"It was an effort to maintain the level of communication that they have had all along," he added.
The meeting came a day after a bomb exploded outside the offices of international monitors in the Serb-controlled town of Zvornik in eastern Bosnia.
The bomb destroyed a pick-up truck belonging to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) but caused no casualties.
The NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) said there was no evidence the bombing was part of an orchestrated campaign to retaliate for the swoop on indicted war criminals.
Colic said after the meeting that the Serb army strongly condemned the arrest operation as outside NATO's peacekeeping mandate.
"We still maintain the view that what SFOR is doing is not regulated by the Dayton (peace) agreement," Colic was quoted as saying by the Bosnian Serb news agency.
He said Serbs and the Serb military believed that SFOR's action was "an attack against the Serb people".
SFOR says "Operation Tango" was within its peacekeeping mandate, which requires soldiers to detain suspects encountered during their regular duties..
SFOR commanders say all the former warring factions are obliged to hand over indicted war criminals under terms of the Dayton peace agreement signed in 1995.

In the past, NATO commanders had been reluctant to go after indicted war criminals, partly because they feared such operations would trigger attacks on peacekeeping troops and disrupt relations with rival armies.
The United Nations, the OSCE and other envoys played down a possible security threat and said they had no plans to evacuate staff members from Serb territory.

A spokesman for the High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, said the bombing would not undermine international resolve to see suspects extradited to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
"Life goes on as normal," Duncan Bullivant told reporters. "We do not see a widespread, orchestrated security problem. We see isolated incidents."

Serb leaders have refrained from inciting the population to take up arms in revenge and have struck a much more cautious tone than in wartime, when they defied Western governments with shelling attacks on Sarajevo and abductions of U.N. peacekeeping soldiers.
The Bosnian Serb military, once the dominant military force in Bosnia, is now strictly supervised by the alliance-led force and its heavy weapons have been placed in storage sites.
